newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Number of U.S. poor is rising, says U.N. report.
newsitem.headline: Number of U.S. poor is rising, says U.N. report.

text.p: The number of people in the United States living in poverty is gradually rising, even though its per capita income of $26,397 is one of the world's highest, a U.N. report said on Thursday.

The percentage of those living below the poverty line rose from 16 percent in 1974 to more than 19 percent in 1994, according to the 1997 Human Development Report, commissioned by the U.N. Development Programme.
It said one in four children in the United States under the age of 18 was income poor, which it called the worst record among leading industrialised countries.
One in five senior citizens in the United States also live in poverty, as well as three out of five single-parent households.

But the report said poverty had also worsened in Australia, Belgium, Britain, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Norway. By contrast, poverty had decreased in Canada, Denmark, France, Italy and Spain.
"These figures only show the extent of poverty in terms of inadequate income," said Richard Jolly, chief coordinator of the report and special adviser to the UNDP administrator.
"Poverty is actually much more complex than that. The real tragedy of human poverty is that it includes deprivation of life choices and opportunities, often over a whole lifetime."
The report also highlighted other statistics showing the United States trailing other industrialised countries in quality of life.

It had the industrialised world's second-highest rate of AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome), with 15.2 cases per 100,000 people. The highest in that category was Spain, with 15.7 cases. The Bahamas topped the list among developing countries with about 142 AIDS cases per 100,000.

The United States also had a short life span by the standards of the industrialised world. The report said it was in 22nd place, with a lifespan of 76.2 years, compared with top-ranked Japan with 79.8 years.

The United States ranked fourth according to the report's Human Development Index, which measures countries' achievements and overall living standards by combining statistics for per capita income, life expectancy and educational attainment.

Canada was in first place for the fourth consecutive year, followed by France and Norway. The United States had been in second spot last year but, according to the report, human development in Canada, France and Norway rose at a faster pace.
